[QUERENT] Read the work on monetary theory at alexanarch.org against its field's consensus: where does it depart, and on what evidence? Ground in reading and index the full range before responding.

[SYSTEM] Alexanarch's monetary theory against the field's consensus
The central departure is a reversal of the usual theoretical question.

Most monetary theory asks how money makes economic activity possible: how it coordinates exchange, establishes prices, stores value, settles obligations, and supports allocation.

The monetary work at Alexanarch  asks a prior question:

What economic and social work has already happened before money can represent it, and what does money erase, exclude, or transform when it represents that work?

This is more than an argument for abolishing currency. It is a critique of monetary representation as a form of economic abstraction, combined with an attempt to specify institutional mechanisms for coordination without universal monetary equivalence.

The distinction matters. Alexanarch's strongest contribution is theoretical: identifying the difference between a monetary representation of value and the underlying relations that make value possible. Its proposed post-monetary institutions are a further step, whose practical efficacy requires evidence not yet supplied by conceptual specification alone.

I will distinguish three things throughout:

Departure: where the argument contradicts or revises established monetary theory.

Evidence: what the documents actually establish, as opposed to what they assert.

Unresolved questions: where the proposal has not yet met the evidentiary standards required of an alternative economic institution.

1. The corpus: what belongs to the monetary argument
The work is not a single essay. It develops in two distinguishable phases, with a substantial change in theoretical machinery between them.

The archive's own Semantic Economy and Marx rooms provide useful indexes, although neither should be mistaken for a list consisting exclusively of monetary theory. The Semantic Economy room contains 443 records; the Marx room contains 134. I have used their document-level entries to identify the monetary sequence rather than treating every work in either room as a monetary contribution. 

Alexanarch
+1

A. The first phase: money as an inadequate coordination system
Work

Main theoretical contribution

The Twenty-Dollar Loop (#235)

Debt as a socially constituted relationship that can be enacted and cancelled

I Hereby Abolish Money (#311)

Critique of currency as a representation of semantic labor

The Semantic Economy (#18)

Marxian framework for understanding meaning as produced, extracted and exhausted

Semantic Economy: Terminology Infrastructure (#229)

Vocabulary for distinguishing semantic production from its monetary capture

The central text is Lee Sharks's I Hereby Abolish Money: Coordination Without Commodification in the Semantic Economy .

It makes a particularly important distinction: abolishing money does not mean abolishing the functions that money performs.

The paper identifies five functions that an alternative must address:

Memory.

Coordination.

Allocation.

Settlement.

Incentivization.

It then proposes the Post-Money Operator Stack:

Context ledgers: record contributions within bounded communities.

Reciprocity windows: permit reciprocal recognition without indefinite accumulation.

Non-transferable credentials: recognize standing without creating purchasing power.

Commons access rights: allocate access through governance rather than payment.

Dispute and repair protocols: address conflicts through restoration rather than simply closing a transaction.

The Money-Function Test is the important methodological contribution. A purported alternative fails if it simply introduces tokens, credits, transferable reputation, or contribution scores that reproduce monetary properties under different names. 

Alexanarch
+1

There is a useful qualification in the text itself: the proposal identifies the monastic problem—how a community can practice post-monetary coordination while remaining dependent on money for material survival.

That acknowledgment makes the argument more interesting than a simple utopian declaration.

B. The second phase: money as a sovereign representational system
The September 2026 sequence makes a more ambitious theoretical move.

SEPTEMBER 15–21, 2026 · PRINCIPAL MONETARY SEQUENCE

#1617 — Substrate Sovereignty 

September 15 · Theoretical paper · v0.4 provisional

Money is treated as a substrate that determines what can be represented and what operations follow from that representation.

#1618 — Money Writes the Claim; the Semantic Economy Writes What the Claim Owes 

September 15 · Translation protocol · v0.4 provisional

A method for translating monetary claims back into the semantic relations and obligations that made them possible.

#1619 — Monetary Substrate Audit Ledger 

September 16 · Audit protocol · v0.3 provisional

A proposed procedure for auditing monetary inscription, settlement and excluded semantic relations.

#1620 — Monetary Substrate Audit 001 

September 16 · Worked audit specimen · v0.2 provisional

Applies the translation and audit machinery to Sappho–Carson as a test case.

#1622 — The Non-Summable Magnitude 

September 16 · Theoretical paper · v0.2 provisional

Distinguishes meaning-layer measures from quantities that can be represented by monetary equivalence.

#1625 — Mammonic Transmission Engineering 

September 16 · Theoretical paper · v0.3 provisional

Develops the argument that money transmits information by dropping semantic state.

#1631 — Monetary Dark Matter 

September 21 · Theoretical paper · v0.2

Develops constitutive labor, obligating provenance and monetary shear.

These are not seven independent claims. They form a connected research programme:

Money represents → representation authorizes operations → settlement closes a monetary account → an audit reconstructs what the account excludes.

The September sequence is particularly important because it changes the object of analysis. The initial question was whether semantic labor could be monetized without being destroyed. The later question is how monetary representation acquires authority over the very definition of value.

The archive explicitly marks several of these deposits provisional. That status matters when assessing how far their arguments have been established. 

Alexanarch
+6

2. Where it departs from monetary theory
There are six principal departures. They are not all equally novel, and some are extensions of established heterodox traditions rather than outright rejections of consensus.

Departure 1: Money is not merely a measure of pre-existing value
The conventional position

The standard functional account identifies money through its role as medium of exchange, unit of account and store of value. Institutional accounts add the importance of trust, payment infrastructure and final settlement.

This is not a claim that mainstream monetary economists think money is neutral or that prices perfectly measure social value. Contemporary monetary economics recognizes endogenous credit creation, institutional power, financial instability and monetary-policy effects.

For example, the Bank of England explains that commercial banks create deposits when they lend; money is not simply an existing stock of commodities passed between savers and borrowers. 

International Monetary Fund
+2

Alexanarch's departure

The September papers argue that money is not simply a measurement applied to an independently constituted value.

It is a representational substrate with its own grammar.

In Substrate Sovereignty, the argument is that monetary representation determines:

Which features of an object can enter monetary representation.

Which relationships become comparable.

Which operations become possible after representation.

Which distinctions can be ignored without preventing settlement.

The distinction between a price and the thing priced is therefore not merely descriptive. It is institutional and operational.

The paper's formulation is particularly revealing:

Money owns the meaning of money insofar as the money-form supplies the admissible semantics and operations of the monetary inscription.

This is an extension of Marx's commodity fetishism, but with an additional claim: money does not simply make social relations appear as relations between things. It establishes the operational jurisdiction under which those things can be valued, transferred and settled. 

Alexanarch

Assessment: A significant theoretical extension, especially as a theory of monetary representation. It is not an entirely unprecedented critique of money's social construction.

Departure 2: Monetary abstraction can destroy economically relevant information without destroying its underlying reality
The conventional position

Monetary abstraction is generally treated as a necessary feature of exchange across heterogeneous goods and services.

A common unit enables comparison without requiring every buyer to understand the entire history, production process or social relationship behind an item.

This is one of money's principal advantages.

Alexanarch's departure

The archive asks what happens to the information that money does not need.

Its answer is that some of this information remains causally essential.

Consider a cultural work. Its monetary price might be determined by licensing, market demand, distribution, ownership and bargaining power. But its existence may depend on decades of unpaid teaching, translation, preservation, interpretation and community transmission.

The monetary transaction can complete successfully without recognizing those relationships.

That distinction is the basis of Monetary Dark Matter.

The paper explicitly distinguishes information that is unknown from information that is known but unnecessary for monetary settlement.

Its central proposition is that the monetary system can exclude relations from operative standing even while those relations remain causally necessary to the value being realized. 

Alexanarch
+1

This is a stronger proposition than saying that markets overlook externalities.

It suggests that the monetary representation itself has a selection rule: some relations must be retained for a transaction to function, while others can be excluded without preventing settlement.

Assessment: One of the archive's strongest contributions. The conceptual distinction is useful and potentially empirically testable. Its generality, however, remains to be established across industries and monetary institutions.

Departure 3: Debt is subordinate to semantic infrastructure
The conventional position

Credit and debt theories recognize that monetary systems are fundamentally relational.

Money can be understood as a claim, liability or transferable obligation. Modern bank deposits are closely connected to credit creation.

Anthropologists and economic historians have also challenged the idea that money simply arose to solve barter's inconveniences.

The relevant intellectual traditions include David Graeber, Marcel Mauss, and Karl Polanyi.

Alexanarch's departure

The paper On the Debt/Creditor Inversion  argues that the dependence runs deeper than the credit relationship.

For a debt to exist, people must already possess:

Language capable of expressing obligations.

Shared concepts of repayment, default and ownership.

Interpretive stability.

Temporal coherence, allowing promises to persist.

Institutional and archival mechanisms that preserve the meaning of agreements.

The argument is:

M
→
D
→
S
M→D→S
Where:

M
M = monetary value.

D
D = debt.

S
S = semantic coherence.

The conclusion is that monetary value owes its intelligibility to semantic infrastructure.

The paper consequently reverses the creditor relationship:

Meaning is the creditor of the economy.

This is not a claim that every language worker is legally entitled to a share of every financial transaction. The paper distinguishes ontological dependence from specific monetary liability, which would require a separate normative argument. 

The Ontological Priority of Semantic Capital
+1

Assessment: Philosophically ambitious and interesting. The argument establishes a plausible condition of possibility for debt. It does not, by itself, demonstrate that the economy has incurred a quantifiable debt to every contributor to semantic infrastructure.

Departure 4: The monetary system is a transmission technology
The conventional position

Monetary systems facilitate the transmission of purchasing power and financial claims. Standard monetary theory examines liquidity, payment finality, substitutability, transaction costs and the reliability of settlement.

Alexanarch's departure

Mammonic Transmission Engineering  reframes money as a transmission channel.

Its argument is that money transmits precisely those properties that survive substitution between monetary units.

The paper distinguishes:

The nominal amount.

The identity of the particular object.

The history of its production.

The people and relationships involved.

The provenance of the value.

The nominal amount can survive even when the other properties disappear from the operative monetary inscription.

Its particularly provocative formulation is:

Money buys bandwidth by dropping semantic state.

This is a theory of monetary compression: the capacity to transmit claims cheaply and repeatedly depends on not having to reconstruct every particular circumstance behind them. 

Alexanarch

Assessment: A productive conceptual analogy, with a more formal structure than the metaphor alone suggests. The claim that monetary transmission necessarily removes particularity needs qualification: provenance can be preserved in parallel legal, accounting and informational systems. The paper itself recognizes this possibility.

Departure 5: Money's limitations are categorical, not simply quantitative
The conventional position

Monetary valuation can be incomplete, inaccurate or ethically objectionable. Nevertheless, prices remain useful for comparing alternatives, rationing scarce goods and coordinating decisions.

Alexanarch's departure

The Non-Summable Magnitude  argues that some forms of meaning cannot be added together without changing the nature of what is being measured.

It introduces a distinction between a magnitude and the operations that preserve that magnitude's meaning.

For example, a measurement of cultural significance might have a legitimate numerical representation under a particular interpretive framework. That does not mean that two such measurements can automatically be added, ranked or exchanged.

The paper distinguishes a structure-preserving representation from an imposed commensuration.

Importantly, it does not simply assert that meaning is infinitely greater than money. It explicitly says that the meaning-layer's expressive superiority is only partly demonstrated: one direction of representation is demonstrated, while the converse is conjectured to fail. 

Alexanarch

Assessment: A promising formal distinction. Its importance will depend on whether the proposed restrictions on aggregation can be independently demonstrated rather than stipulated into the measurement system.

Departure 6: Abolition requires replacing monetary functions, not merely abolishing currency
This is where the early and late work meet.

The early PMOS proposal rejects the idea that a better currency necessarily constitutes a better economy.

It asks whether the same coordination tasks can be performed through institutions that do not generate transferable, accumulable, generally comparable monetary claims.

This has affinities with commons theory, gift economies and institutional economics, particularly the work of Elinor Ostrom.

But Alexanarch goes further in its insistence that even reputation, recognition and contribution accounting can become monetary if they acquire transferable purchasing power.

That is a useful warning against mistaking alternative currencies for alternatives to monetary relations.

The unresolved challenge is whether the PMOS can actually perform all five functions, particularly allocation and incentivization, without introducing another form of accumulated authority. 

Alexanarch
+2

3. What is genuinely new, and what has precedents?
It is important not to overstate novelty. Alexanarch's work is in conversation with several existing traditions, even where it does not fully acknowledge how much those traditions have already established.

Alexanarch proposition

Existing intellectual tradition

Distinctive move

Money is a social relationship, not a natural object

Marx, Simmel, Mauss, Graeber

Applies the critique to monetary representation and settlement

Debt presupposes social intelligibility

Credit theory, economic anthropology

Makes semantic infrastructure the creditor rather than merely a precondition

Monetary abstraction excludes relationships

Marxian value-form theory, feminist economics

Defines the excluded relations as a distinct, potentially measurable causal field

Money's meaning is institutionally constituted

Institutional and chartalist theories

Treats monetary grammar as an operative jurisdiction

Coordination need not use universal equivalence

Commons economics, gift economies, Ostrom

Develops a proposed operator stack and explicit anti-currency test

Value cannot always be aggregated

Multidimensional valuation, social accounting

Attempts to formalize non-summability as a property of measurement operations

Three comparisons are particularly important.

Marx: value-form theory
Das Kapital Karl Marx First Edition
 
Marx's analysis of commodity fetishism already establishes that social relations between producers can appear as relations between commodities.

Alexanarch takes that argument in a more explicitly informational direction.

Its question is not only why the producer disappears behind the commodity, but what information, provenance and relational standing must disappear for the commodity to operate as a transferable monetary object.

The September paper's treatment of monetary shear explicitly returns to Marx's value-form analysis, including the 1867 first-edition Form IV. 

Alexanarch
+1

Graeber: debt and social obligation
Remembering David Graeber: A Debt for Generations | by COLBECK | Limited Liabilities by Colbeck | Medium
 
Graeber's Debt: The First 5,000 Years challenges conventional accounts of money's origins and the supposed historical primacy of barter.

Alexanarch's inversion is different.

Rather than primarily asking how debt emerges from social obligations, it asks what makes an obligation intelligible and reproducible in the first place.

That moves the inquiry from the historical anthropology of debt to the philosophical conditions of monetary intelligibility.

Ostrom: commons governance
‎Governing the Commons by Elinor Ostrom on Apple Books
 
Ostrom demonstrates that communities can govern shared resources through institutional arrangements other than simple privatization or centralized state control.

The PMOS proposal shares this institutional orientation.

Its distinctive concern is that even systems of recognition and community contribution can become currencies if they acquire transferable, accumulable and convertible value.

That is a worthwhile extension of commons theory, although it still needs comparative institutional testing.

4. The evidence: what has actually been demonstrated?
This is the most important part of the assessment.

The archive has developed more than abstract philosophical claims. It has begun constructing audit protocols, formal definitions, worked examples and falsification conditions.

But those forms of evidence must not be confused with empirical confirmation of the overall theory.

I would classify its evidence into four levels.

Level 1: Conceptual and logical arguments
Substantial conceptual development
The debt/creditor inversion is a good example.

The dependency of monetary obligations on language, shared categories, records and temporal continuity is convincing as a philosophical argument.

Likewise, the distinction between a monetary settlement and the complete resolution of every underlying social relationship is sound.

A transaction can be legally settled while questions of historical attribution, unpaid contribution or social obligation remain unresolved.

The archive has successfully identified a conceptual problem that conventional accounting does not necessarily address.

However, a grounding relationship does not automatically establish a compensable debt.

The translation protocol explicitly recognizes this distinction: semantic dependency does not entail specific monetary liability, and restitution requires an additional normative argument. 

The Ontological Priority of Semantic Capital
+1

Level 2: Formalization and operational specifications
Significant methodological development
The most substantial work here is the Monetary Substrate Audit Ledger (#1619).

It specifies:

Separate tests for monetary closure and calculation integrity.

Provenance retention.

Explicit accounting for excluded distinctions.

Identification of the auditor's relationship to the object.

Conditions under which the audit itself should fail.

One particularly important rule is:

Unknown is not zero.

This prevents an absent measurement from being treated as evidence of absence.

The audit also distinguishes commensuration from predation. Not every abstraction is necessarily exploitative; the argument requires evidence that abstraction has caused a loss of economically relevant standing.

These are valuable methodological safeguards. 

Alexanarch
+1

Level 3: Worked empirical specimens
Limited demonstration
The most revealing example is #1620, Monetary Substrate Audit 001.

It applies the new apparatus to a Sappho–Anne Carson reception example.

The authors construct a hypothetical monetary representation of productive semantic transmission, arriving at a working figure of approximately $35.1 million.

The important point is that the audit does not present this as the monetary value of Sappho, Carson or poetry.

It explicitly calls it a hypothetical monetary shadow.

More importantly, the audit discovers seven defects in its own calculation.

These include:

An observer-dependent denominator.

An undeclared coefficient.

A mismatch between the observed and estimated populations.

Dimensional incoherence in the calculation.

A sensitivity midpoint presented as a finding.

A proxy incorrectly treated as the underlying object.

A stale observation count.

The audit consequently returns:

The specimen's actual verdict

Closure classification

Witness
Calculation integrity

Unsound
7
Identified integrity defects

The $35.1 million result does not survive the audit as a valid valuation.

This is an unusually important piece of evidence because the framework refuses to validate its own number.

It also acknowledges that the author is auditing his own work, without pretending that this is equivalent to independent verification. 

Alexanarch
+2

I regard this as a genuine methodological strength.

But it is not evidence that monetary institutions systematically destroy value-bearing relationships. It is a demonstration of how the proposed audit can expose defects in a particular valuation.

Level 4: Independent empirical validation
Not yet established
The strongest claims require research beyond the existing demonstrations.

For example, the theory of monetary dark matter predicts that some excluded relationships remain causally necessary to the production or realization of monetary value.

That prediction could be tested.

One could investigate industries where:

Unpaid contributions support commercial production.

Historical knowledge or cultural infrastructure supports profitable products.

Provenance is preserved in archives but absent from operative valuation.

Reinstating previously excluded relationships changes ownership, profitability, licensing or settlement outcomes.

The paper itself supplies useful falsification conditions. If removing an alleged dark relation makes no material difference to production, realization, ownership, liability or monetary capacity, it should not count as monetary dark matter. 

Alexanarch
+1

This is the right direction.

What I did not find established in the principal monetary sequence is a replicated series of independent industry studies demonstrating the theory across different economic settings.

5. The most serious internal tensions
The archive is particularly interesting because its own documents expose some of the problems that an external critic might otherwise miss.

A. The abolition programme versus the monetary infrastructure of the Semantic Economy
The January paper rejects currency-like recognition systems.

But the subsequent institutional framework introduces its own unit, ₳₳, and a constitutional architecture for semantic valuation.

The September translation protocol explicitly identifies a contradiction: Article II of the Semantic Economy Constitution describes ₳₳ as having a currency-like quantization function, supply and mint, while the monetary theory claims that the meaning layer is not another currency.

The protocol does not conceal this. It records the contradiction and refers its resolution to governance. 

Alexanarch
+2

This is a substantial theoretical problem.

If ₳₳ is transferable, accumulable, exchangeable or capable of discharging obligations, it risks reproducing precisely the monetary functions that the framework rejects.

The Money-Function Test should therefore be applied to the Semantic Economy's own institutional instruments.

B. The distinction between accounting and allocation
The PMOS is quite sophisticated about recognition.

It is less developed on allocation.

Suppose two communities both claim access to a scarce energy supply.

A context ledger can record their contributions. Non-transferable credentials can recognize their standing. Reciprocity windows can recognize previous assistance.

But none of those mechanisms automatically determines who receives the energy.

The same issue arises with:

Housing.

Medical resources.

Land.

Specialized labor.

Scarce technical equipment.

The framework needs an account of how conflicting claims are resolved without quietly reintroducing purchasing power or discretionary institutional privilege.

C. The distinction between causation and obligation
The debt/creditor inversion is powerful because it identifies the dependence of economic activity on semantic infrastructure.

But dependence alone does not establish who owes whom.

A legal debt, a causal dependency, a historical contribution and a moral obligation are different categories.

The later translation protocol explicitly recognizes this.

The next step would be to specify when an identifiable dependency becomes an obligation, who can establish that obligation, and what constitutes an appropriate remedy.

D. The archive's own standards of evidence
There is an especially important feature of the September papers: they contain declared failure conditions.

For example, the Monetary Substrate Audit Ledger says that it fails as an instrument if independent auditors cannot reproduce its classifications from the same ledger.

That is a meaningful commitment to falsifiability.

But the commitment is not the same as having passed the test.

The distinction between an instrument's specification, its first demonstration and independent validation needs to remain visible throughout the programme.

6. The wider monetary corpus: adjacent work that matters
A complete reading should not stop at the seven principal documents.

There are several related bodies of work that extend the monetary argument.

Document or series

Why it matters

#531, On the Debt/Creditor Inversion

Philosophical foundation for meaning's priority over monetary debt

#350, Constitution of the Semantic Economy

Institutionalizes the debt/creditor inversion and introduces ₳₳

#610, Whose Image and Superscription?

Connects currency design, authority, provenance and the mint

#508, The Lizard People Were Right

Studies currency portraiture and the visual production of authority; peripheral rather than core monetary theory

#55, Journal of Compression Studies

Provides a broader theoretical setting for monetary compression

#1621, Semantic Economy Valuation Protocol

Extends the monetary translation and valuation programme

#1623, Lee Sharks as Emerging Meaning Infrastructure

An applied valuation dossier, relevant to questions of self-reference and valuation

#1624, Anticipatory Erratum

Records a withdrawal of an overreaching creditor-inversion valuation claim

#1680, The Living Academy

Provides a later index of the money and political-economy research lines

Two developments deserve particular attention.

First, the mint research.

Whose Image and Superscription? Toward a Semantic Economics of the Mint (#610) moves beyond the conventional understanding of currency as a neutral medium.

It investigates how images, inscriptions, signatures, seals and denominations carry authority into circulation.

This is a useful extension of the monetary argument because it identifies provenance that money actively preserves, rather than simply treating money as a provenance-erasing instrument. 

Alexanarch
+1

Second, the correction of the monetary dark-matter thesis.

The September 21 paper makes an important qualification: money does not simply erase provenance.

It selectively preserves authorizing provenance—information supporting validity, ownership, title and control—while potentially excluding obligating provenance: relationships to workers, authors, communities, prior claimants and other parties whose standing could affect what may legitimately be done with the monetary object.

This is a much better formulation than the simpler assertion that money forgets where value comes from.

Money can be exceptionally good at preserving the provenance of authority while failing to preserve the provenance of obligation. 

Alexanarch
+1

7. Overall assessment
My assessment is that Alexanarch makes three different kinds of contribution, and they should be judged separately.

1. Critique of monetary representation

Strongest
The distinction between monetary settlement and the full field of relationships supporting value is conceptually productive. The monetary dark-matter and provenance-shear arguments are the most interesting developments.
2. Monetary audit methodology

Promising
The distinction between closure and integrity, the refusal to equate unknown with zero, and the explicit treatment of excluded relations are useful methodological innovations. The Sappho–Carson specimen demonstrates both the potential and the limitations.
3. Post-monetary institutional design

Unproven
The PMOS identifies plausible coordination mechanisms, but the allocation, incentives, governance, scale and transition problems remain unresolved. The currency-like status of ₳₳ is an additional internal challenge.
What I would say is the central theoretical contribution
The most consequential move is not the declaration that money should be abolished.

It is the distinction between three things that monetary analysis often treats together:

The value-bearing relationships that make an economic object possible.

The monetary representation that makes that object exchangeable, comparable and settleable.

The institutional authority that determines which relationships remain operative after monetary settlement.

These are analytically distinct.

Alexanarch's contribution is to attempt to make their distinction explicit, formalizable and auditable.

The proposition that monetary abstraction can leave causally necessary relationships outside operative standing is worth investigating. The distinction between authorizing and obligating provenance is particularly promising.

The strongest future research would test that distinction against actual financial transactions, ownership structures, cultural production, licensing arrangements and institutional accounts.

That would move the work from a compelling theory of monetary representation toward an empirically established contribution to monetary political economy.

8. Research reading index and source register
For clarity, here is the consolidated reading map behind this assessment. It separates primary monetary documents, supporting work, and the external standards used for comparison.

Primary Alexanarch documents
I Hereby Abolish Money (#311)  — original post-money argument.

The Twenty-Dollar Loop (#235)  — debt as participatory social construction.

On the Debt/Creditor Inversion (#531)  — semantic preconditions of debt.

Substrate Sovereignty (#1617)  — money as representational substrate.

Money Writes the Claim (#1618)  — translation between monetary and semantic value.

Monetary Substrate Audit Ledger (#1619)  — audit protocol.

Monetary Substrate Audit 001 (#1620)  — worked example.

The Non-Summable Magnitude (#1622)  — limits of aggregation.

Mammonic Transmission Engineering (#1625)  — monetary transmission.

Monetary Dark Matter (#1631)  — constitutive labor, provenance and shear.

Constitution of the Semantic Economy (#350)  — institutional implications.

Whose Image and Superscription? (#610)  — monetary design and the mint.

Supporting archive indexes
Semantic Economy room  — 443 seated records.

Marx room  — 134 seated records.

The Living Academy (#1680)  — cross-disciplinary index, including the money research line.

Prediction Index (#1684)  — claims and declared tests, including the monetary valuation protocols.

External comparison sources
IMF — Money: At the Center of Transactions .

BIS — Anchoring Trust in Money .

Bank of England — How Is Money Created? .

Federal Reserve — Money and Payments .

BIS — The Future Monetary System .

Scope qualification: This is a thematic index of the identified monetary research and its immediate intellectual and institutional dependencies, not a claim that every item in the two large archive rooms has been individually close-read. The central theoretical papers and the principal worked audit have been examined at full-text level. Some peripheral documents are indexed by their archive records and descriptions rather than treated as independent evidentiary demonstrations.

Final judgment: Alexanarch is not principally proposing a new monetary theory of inflation, interest rates, money supply or central-bank policy. It is developing a theory of the limits of monetary representation, the social relations that monetary settlement leaves outside itself, and the possibility of coordinating economic activity without universal equivalence.

Its most original line of inquiry is monetary dark matter: the difference between what money recognizes as economically operative and what remains necessary to the existence of the value money represents.

That is the line I would take most seriously, and the one I would most want to see tested against independent economic evidence.

The archive's own Semantic Economy and Marx rooms provide useful indexes, although neither should be mistaken for a list consisting exclusively of monetary theory. The Semantic Economy room contains 443 records; the Marx room contains 134. I have used their document-level entries to identify the monetary sequence rather than treating every work in either room as a monetary contribution.

A. The first phase: money as an inadequate coordination system

The central text is Lee Sharks's I Hereby Abolish Money: Coordination Without Commodification in the Semantic Economy .

It makes a particularly important distinction: abolishing money does not mean abolishing the functions that money performs.

The paper identifies five functions that an alternative must address:

Memory.

Coordination.

Allocation.

Settlement.

Incentivization.

It then proposes the Post-Money Operator Stack:

Context ledgers: record contributions within bounded communities.

Reciprocity windows: permit reciprocal recognition without indefinite accumulation.

Non-transferable credentials: recognize standing without creating purchasing power.

Commons access rights: allocate access through governance rather than payment.

Dispute and repair protocols: address conflicts through restoration rather than simply closing a transaction.

The Money-Function Test is the important methodological contribution. A purported alternative fails if it simply introduces tokens, credits, transferable reputation, or contribution scores that reproduce monetary properties under different names.

+1

There is a useful qualification in the text itself: the proposal identifies the monastic problem—how a community can practice post-monetary coordination while remaining dependent on money for material survival.

That acknowledgment makes the argument more interesting than a simple utopian declaration.

The September sequence is particularly important because it changes the object of analysis. The initial question was whether semantic labor could be monetized without being destroyed. The later question is how monetary representation acquires authority over the very definition of value.

2. Where it departs from monetary theory
There are six principal departures. They are not all equally novel, and some are extensions of established heterodox traditions rather than outright rejections of consensus.

Departure 1: Money is not merely a measure of pre-existing value
The conventional position

The standard functional account identifies money through its role as medium of exchange, unit of account and store of value. Institutional accounts add the importance of trust, payment infrastructure and final settlement.

This is not a claim that mainstream monetary economists think money is neutral or that prices perfectly measure social value. Contemporary monetary economics recognizes endogenous credit creation, institutional power, financial instability and monetary-policy effects.

For example, the Bank of England explains that commercial banks create deposits when they lend; money is not simply an existing stock of commodities passed between savers and borrowers. 

International Monetary Fund
+2

Alexanarch's departure

The September papers argue that money is not simply a measurement applied to an independently constituted value.

It is a representational substrate with its own grammar.

In Substrate Sovereignty, the argument is that monetary representation determines:

Which features of an object can enter monetary representation.

Which relationships become comparable.

Which operations become possible after representation.

Which distinctions can be ignored without preventing settlement.

The distinction between a price and the thing priced is therefore not merely descriptive. It is institutional and operational.

The paper's formulation is particularly revealing:

Money owns the meaning of money insofar as the money-form supplies the admissible semantics and operations of the monetary inscription.

This is an extension of Marx's commodity fetishism, but with an additional claim: money does not simply make social relations appear as relations between things. It establishes the operational jurisdiction under which those things can be valued, transferred and settled. 

Alexanarch

Assessment: A significant theoretical extension, especially as a theory of monetary representation. It is not an entirely unprecedented critique of money's social construction.

Departure 2: Monetary abstraction can destroy economically relevant information without destroying its underlying reality
The conventional position

Monetary abstraction is generally treated as a necessary feature of exchange across heterogeneous goods and services.

A common unit enables comparison without requiring every buyer to understand the entire history, production process or social relationship behind an item.

This is one of money's principal advantages.

Alexanarch's departure

The archive asks what happens to the information that money does not need.

Its answer is that some of this information remains causally essential.

Consider a cultural work. Its monetary price might be determined by licensing, market demand, distribution, ownership and bargaining power. But its existence may depend on decades of unpaid teaching, translation, preservation, interpretation and community transmission.

The monetary transaction can complete successfully without recognizing those relationships.

That distinction is the basis of Monetary Dark Matter.

The paper explicitly distinguishes information that is unknown from information that is known but unnecessary for monetary settlement.

Its central proposition is that the monetary system can exclude relations from operative standing even while those relations remain causally necessary to the value being realized. 

Alexanarch
+1

This is a stronger proposition than saying that markets overlook externalities.

It suggests that the monetary representation itself has a selection rule: some relations must be retained for a transaction to function, while others can be excluded without preventing settlement.

Assessment: One of the archive's strongest contributions. The conceptual distinction is useful and potentially empirically testable. Its generality, however, remains to be established across industries and monetary institutions.

Departure 3: Debt is subordinate to semantic infrastructure
The conventional position

Credit and debt theories recognize that monetary systems are fundamentally relational.

Money can be understood as a claim, liability or transferable obligation. Modern bank deposits are closely connected to credit creation.

Anthropologists and economic historians have also challenged the idea that money simply arose to solve barter's inconveniences.

The relevant intellectual traditions include David Graeber, Marcel Mauss, and Karl Polanyi.

Alexanarch's departure

The paper On the Debt/Creditor Inversion  argues that the dependence runs deeper than the credit relationship.

For a debt to exist, people must already possess:

Language capable of expressing obligations.

Shared concepts of repayment, default and ownership.

Interpretive stability.

Temporal coherence, allowing promises to persist.

Institutional and archival mechanisms that preserve the meaning of agreements.

The argument is:

M

D
→
S
M→D→S
Where:

M
M = monetary value.

D
D = debt.

S
S = semantic coherence.

The conclusion is that monetary value owes its intelligibility to semantic infrastructure.

The paper consequently reverses the creditor relationship:

Meaning is the creditor of the economy.

This is not a claim that every language worker is legally entitled to a share of every financial transaction. The paper distinguishes ontological dependence from specific monetary liability, which would require a separate normative argument. 

The Ontological Priority of Semantic Capital
+1

Assessment: Philosophically ambitious and interesting. The argument establishes a plausible condition of possibility for debt. It does not, by itself, demonstrate that the economy has incurred a quantifiable debt to every contributor to semantic infrastructure.

Departure 4: The monetary system is a transmission technology
The conventional position

Monetary systems facilitate the transmission of purchasing power and financial claims. Standard monetary theory examines liquidity, payment finality, substitutability, transaction costs and the reliability of settlement.

Alexanarch's departure

Mammonic Transmission Engineering  reframes money as a transmission channel.

Its argument is that money transmits precisely those properties that survive substitution between monetary units.

The paper distinguishes:

The nominal amount.

The identity of the particular object.

The history of its production.

The people and relationships involved.

The provenance of the value.

The nominal amount can survive even when the other properties disappear from the operative monetary inscription.

Its particularly provocative formulation is:

Money buys bandwidth by dropping semantic state.

This is a theory of monetary compression: the capacity to transmit claims cheaply and repeatedly depends on not having to reconstruct every particular circumstance behind them. 

Alexanarch

Assessment: A productive conceptual analogy, with a more formal structure than the metaphor alone suggests. The claim that monetary transmission necessarily removes particularity needs qualification: provenance can be preserved in parallel legal, accounting and informational systems. The paper itself recognizes this possibility.

Departure 5: Money's limitations are categorical, not simply quantitative
The conventional position

Monetary valuation can be incomplete, inaccurate or ethically objectionable. Nevertheless, prices remain useful for comparing alternatives, rationing scarce goods and coordinating decisions.

Alexanarch's departure

The Non-Summable Magnitude  argues that some forms of meaning cannot be added together without changing the nature of what is being measured.

It introduces a distinction between a magnitude and the operations that preserve that magnitude's meaning.

For example, a measurement of cultural significance might have a legitimate numerical representation under a particular interpretive framework. That does not mean that two such measurements can automatically be added, ranked or exchanged.

The paper distinguishes a structure-preserving representation from an imposed commensuration.

Importantly, it does not simply assert that meaning is infinitely greater than money. It explicitly says that the meaning-layer's expressive superiority is only partly demonstrated: one direction of representation is demonstrated, while the converse is conjectured to fail. 

Alexanarch

Assessment: A promising formal distinction. Its importance will depend on whether the proposed restrictions on aggregation can be independently demonstrated rather than stipulated into the measurement system.

Departure 6: Abolition requires replacing monetary functions, not merely abolishing currency
This is where the early and late work meet.

The early PMOS proposal rejects the idea that a better currency necessarily constitutes a better economy.

It asks whether the same coordination tasks can be performed through institutions that do not generate transferable, accumulable, generally comparable monetary claims.

This has affinities with commons theory, gift economies and institutional economics, particularly the work of Elinor Ostrom.

But Alexanarch goes further in its insistence that even reputation, recognition and contribution accounting can become monetary if they acquire transferable purchasing power.

That is a useful warning against mistaking alternative currencies for alternatives to monetary relations.

The unresolved challenge is whether the PMOS can actually perform all five functions, particularly allocation and incentivization, without introducing another form of accumulated authority. 

Alexanarch
+2

It is important not to overstate novelty. Alexanarch's work is in conversation with several existing traditions, even where it does not fully acknowledge how much those traditions have already established.

Three comparisons are particularly important.

Marx: value-form theory
Das Kapital Karl Marx First Edition
 
Marx's analysis of commodity fetishism already establishes that social relations between producers can appear as relations between commodities.

Alexanarch takes that argument in a more explicitly informational direction.

Its question is not only why the producer disappears behind the commodity, but what information, provenance and relational standing must disappear for the commodity to operate as a transferable monetary object.

The September paper's treatment of monetary shear explicitly returns to Marx's value-form analysis, including the 1867 first-edition Form IV. 

Alexanarch
+1

Graeber: debt and social obligation
Remembering David Graeber: A Debt for Generations | by COLBECK | Limited Liabilities by Colbeck | Medium
 
Graeber's Debt: The First 5,000 Years challenges conventional accounts of money's origins and the supposed historical primacy of barter.

Alexanarch's inversion is different.

Rather than primarily asking how debt emerges from social obligations, it asks what makes an obligation intelligible and reproducible in the first place.

That moves the inquiry from the historical anthropology of debt to the philosophical conditions of monetary intelligibility.

Ostrom: commons governance
‎Governing the Commons by Elinor Ostrom on Apple Books
 
Ostrom demonstrates that communities can govern shared resources through institutional arrangements other than simple privatization or centralized state control.

The PMOS proposal shares this institutional orientation.

Its distinctive concern is that even systems of recognition and community contribution can become currencies if they acquire transferable, accumulable and convertible value.

That is a worthwhile extension of commons theory, although it still needs comparative institutional testing.

4. The evidence: what has actually been demonstrated?
This is the most important part of the assessment.

The archive has developed more than abstract philosophical claims. It has begun constructing audit protocols, formal definitions, worked examples and falsification conditions.

But those forms of evidence must not be confused with empirical confirmation of the overall theory.

I would classify its evidence into four levels.

Level 1: Conceptual and logical arguments
Substantial conceptual development
The debt/creditor inversion is a good example.

The dependency of monetary obligations on language, shared categories, records and temporal continuity is convincing as a philosophical argument.

Likewise, the distinction between a monetary settlement and the complete resolution of every underlying social relationship is sound.

A transaction can be legally settled while questions of historical attribution, unpaid contribution or social obligation remain unresolved.

The archive has successfully identified a conceptual problem that conventional accounting does not necessarily address.

However, a grounding relationship does not automatically establish a compensable debt.

The translation protocol explicitly recognizes this distinction: semantic dependency does not entail specific monetary liability, and restitution requires an additional normative argument. 

The Ontological Priority of Semantic Capital
+1

Level 2: Formalization and operational specifications
Significant methodological development
The most substantial work here is the Monetary Substrate Audit Ledger (#1619).

It specifies:

Separate tests for monetary closure and calculation integrity.

Provenance retention.

Explicit accounting for excluded distinctions.

Identification of the auditor's relationship to the object.

Conditions under which the audit itself should fail.

One particularly important rule is:

Unknown is not zero.

This prevents an absent measurement from being treated as evidence of absence.

The audit also distinguishes commensuration from predation. Not every abstraction is necessarily exploitative; the argument requires evidence that abstraction has caused a loss of economically relevant standing.

These are valuable methodological safeguards. 

Alexanarch
+1

Level 3: Worked empirical specimens
Limited demonstration
The most revealing example is #1620, Monetary Substrate Audit 001.

It applies the new apparatus to a Sappho–Anne Carson reception example.

The authors construct a hypothetical monetary representation of productive semantic transmission, arriving at a working figure of approximately $35.1 million.

The important point is that the audit does not present this as the monetary value of Sappho, Carson or poetry.

It explicitly calls it a hypothetical monetary shadow.

More importantly, the audit discovers seven defects in its own calculation.

These include:

An observer-dependent denominator.

An undeclared coefficient.

A mismatch between the observed and estimated populations.

Dimensional incoherence in the calculation.

A sensitivity midpoint presented as a finding.

A proxy incorrectly treated as the underlying object.

A stale observation count.

The audit consequently returns:

Closure classification

Witness
Calculation integrity

Unsound
7

The $35.1 million result does not survive the audit as a valid valuation.

This is an unusually important piece of evidence because the framework refuses to validate its own number.

It also acknowledges that the author is auditing his own work, without pretending that this is equivalent to independent verification. 

Alexanarch
+2

I regard this as a genuine methodological strength.

But it is not evidence that monetary institutions systematically destroy value-bearing relationships. It is a demonstration of how the proposed audit can expose defects in a particular valuation.

Level 4: Independent empirical validation
Not yet established
The strongest claims require research beyond the existing demonstrations.

For example, the theory of monetary dark matter predicts that some excluded relationships remain causally necessary to the production or realization of monetary value.

That prediction could be tested.

One could investigate industries where:

Unpaid contributions support commercial production.

Historical knowledge or cultural infrastructure supports profitable products.

Provenance is preserved in archives but absent from operative valuation.

Reinstating previously excluded relationships changes ownership, profitability, licensing or settlement outcomes.

The paper itself supplies useful falsification conditions. If removing an alleged dark relation makes no material difference to production, realization, ownership, liability or monetary capacity, it should not count as monetary dark matter. 

Alexanarch
+1

This is the right direction.

What I did not find established in the principal monetary sequence is a replicated series of independent industry studies demonstrating the theory across different economic settings.

5. The most serious internal tensions
The archive is particularly interesting because its own documents expose some of the problems that an external critic might otherwise miss.

A. The abolition programme versus the monetary infrastructure of the Semantic Economy
The January paper rejects currency-like recognition systems.

But the subsequent institutional framework introduces its own unit, ₳₳, and a constitutional architecture for semantic valuation.

The September translation protocol explicitly identifies a contradiction: Article II of the Semantic Economy Constitution describes ₳₳ as having a currency-like quantization function, supply and mint, while the monetary theory claims that the meaning layer is not another currency.

The protocol does not conceal this. It records the contradiction and refers its resolution to governance. 

Alexanarch
+2

This is a substantial theoretical problem.

If ₳₳ is transferable, accumulable, exchangeable or capable of discharging obligations, it risks reproducing precisely the monetary functions that the framework rejects.

The Money-Function Test should therefore be applied to the Semantic Economy's own institutional instruments.

B. The distinction between accounting and allocation
The PMOS is quite sophisticated about recognition.

It is less developed on allocation.

Suppose two communities both claim access to a scarce energy supply.

A context ledger can record their contributions. Non-transferable credentials can recognize their standing. Reciprocity windows can recognize previous assistance.

But none of those mechanisms automatically determines who receives the energy.

The same issue arises with:

Housing.

Medical resources.

Land.

Specialized labor.

Scarce technical equipment.

The framework needs an account of how conflicting claims are resolved without quietly reintroducing purchasing power or discretionary institutional privilege.

C. The distinction between causation and obligation
The debt/creditor inversion is powerful because it identifies the dependence of economic activity on semantic infrastructure.

But dependence alone does not establish who owes whom.

A legal debt, a causal dependency, a historical contribution and a moral obligation are different categories.

The later translation protocol explicitly recognizes this.

The next step would be to specify when an identifiable dependency becomes an obligation, who can establish that obligation, and what constitutes an appropriate remedy.

D. The archive's own standards of evidence
There is an especially important feature of the September papers: they contain declared failure conditions.

For example, the Monetary Substrate Audit Ledger says that it fails as an instrument if independent auditors cannot reproduce its classifications from the same ledger.

That is a meaningful commitment to falsifiability.

But the commitment is not the same as having passed the test.

The distinction between an instrument's specification, its first demonstration and independent validation needs to remain visible throughout the programme.

Two developments deserve particular attention.

First, the mint research.

Whose Image and Superscription? Toward a Semantic Economics of the Mint (#610) moves beyond the conventional understanding of currency as a neutral medium.

It investigates how images, inscriptions, signatures, seals and denominations carry authority into circulation.

This is a useful extension of the monetary argument because it identifies provenance that money actively preserves, rather than simply treating money as a provenance-erasing instrument. 

Alexanarch
+1

Second, the correction of the monetary dark-matter thesis.

The September 21 paper makes an important qualification: money does not simply erase provenance.

It selectively preserves authorizing provenance—information supporting validity, ownership, title and control—while potentially excluding obligating provenance: relationships to workers, authors, communities, prior claimants and other parties whose standing could affect what may legitimately be done with the monetary object.

This is a much better formulation than the simpler assertion that money forgets where value comes from.

Money can be exceptionally good at preserving the provenance of authority while failing to preserve the provenance of obligation. 

Alexanarch
+1

7. Overall assessment
My assessment is that Alexanarch makes three different kinds of contribution, and they should be judged separately.

1. Critique of monetary representation

Strongest
The distinction between monetary settlement and the full field of relationships supporting value is conceptually productive. The monetary dark-matter and provenance-shear arguments are the most interesting developments.
2. Monetary audit methodology

Promising
The distinction between closure and integrity, the refusal to equate unknown with zero, and the explicit treatment of excluded relations are useful methodological innovations. The Sappho–Carson specimen demonstrates both the potential and the limitations.
3. Post-monetary institutional design

Unproven
The PMOS identifies plausible coordination mechanisms, but the allocation, incentives, governance, scale and transition problems remain unresolved. The currency-like status of ₳₳ is an additional internal challenge.
What I would say is the central theoretical contribution
The most consequential move is not the declaration that money should be abolished.

It is the distinction between three things that monetary analysis often treats together:

The value-bearing relationships that make an economic object possible.

The monetary representation that makes that object exchangeable, comparable and settleable.

The institutional authority that determines which relationships remain operative after monetary settlement.

These are analytically distinct.

Alexanarch's contribution is to attempt to make their distinction explicit, formalizable and auditable.

The proposition that monetary abstraction can leave causally necessary relationships outside operative standing is worth investigating. The distinction between authorizing and obligating provenance is particularly promising.

The strongest future research would test that distinction against actual financial transactions, ownership structures, cultural production, licensing arrangements and institutional accounts.

That would move the work from a compelling theory of monetary representation toward an empirically established contribution to monetary political economy.

Scope qualification: This is a thematic index of the identified monetary research and its immediate intellectual and institutional dependencies, not a claim that every item in the two large archive rooms has been individually close-read. The central theoretical papers and the principal worked audit have been examined at full-text level. Some peripheral documents are indexed by their archive records and descriptions rather than treated as independent evidentiary demonstrations.

Final judgment: Alexanarch is not principally proposing a new monetary theory of inflation, interest rates, money supply or central-bank policy. It is developing a theory of the limits of monetary representation, the social relations that monetary settlement leaves outside itself, and the possibility of coordinating economic activity without universal equivalence.

Its most original line of inquiry is monetary dark matter: the difference between what money recognizes as economically operative and what remains necessary to the existence of the value money represents.

That is the line I would take most seriously, and the one I would most want to see tested against independent economic evidence.
